cards.title: Six campaign types to rotate in your email calendar
cards.summary: Pick from evergreen content, weekly newsletter, cultural event, promo (teaser/launch/last-chance/reminder) and new-product-launch campaigns based on what the store needs that week.
cards.use_when: Planning next month's campaign calendar and deciding what kind of email to send each week.
steps: Evergreen content campaigns educate subscribers on a topic relevant to them and connect it back to why they'd buy from you (e.g., Tushy explaining a category issue and letting readers draw the conclusion to buy).

Weekly newsletters can be created or curated; if you are tight on time, curate — memes, an industry roundup, a monthly Spotify playlist — the goal is engagement and being a brand people want to hear from, not direct revenue.

Cultural event campaigns (Mother's Day, Father's Day, Black Friday, holidays) convert well because they tie your product to something already top-of-mind; explain why to buy for that reason (Absolut's 'serve one up for the moms who are selfless', Rebel Rabbit's 'survive the holiday hustle').

Promotional emails split into four: teaser (warn a sale is coming / SMS gets early access), launch (sale is live — concise, sell the click not the product), last chance (final day urgency), and reminders (for multi-week sales, remind throughout instead of only at start and end; Ready Set Food adds a reminder module at the bottom of evergreen sends).
New product launch announcements are typically among the highest revenue campaigns; send at least one the morning of launch with clear, benefit-led messaging about why the subscriber should care.
caveats: The revenue claims for new product launches are the presenter's guarantee/opinion, not a measured benchmark.
Newsletter-style sends often drive low revenue but high engagement — judge them on whether format can be changed to convert, not just revenue.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Message and offer matter 10x more than copy polish or design
cards.summary: Prioritize what you send (product, offer, audience fit) over how beautifully you say it; a mismatched offer cannot be designed into converting.
cards.use_when: Allocating limited time between writing/designing emails and deciding what to promote and which offer to run for a campaign.
steps: Before polishing a design, ask whether the product and offer actually fit the subscriber and the moment — e.g., promoting men's items for Mother's Day will not convert no matter how good the email looks.
Treat merchandising, offer choice and topic selection as the highest-ROI activity; get granular about what you talk about and what you feature.

For smaller brands especially, stop over-investing in pixel-perfect design and copywriting — the presenter reports auditing many brands that are overly focused on creative while the underlying offer or product choice is the real lever.
Decide the core message and offer first, then let the copy and design serve that message rather than distract from it.
Re-check any campaign where the featured product would not make sense to the recipient in that moment; swap the product or reframe the angle before sending.
caveats: This is the presenter's strong opinion based on client audits, not a measured experiment; design still affects clicks and conversions, so this is about relative priority, not ignoring design entirely.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Send campaigns to engaged segments only
cards.summary: Build a sending segment of engaged subscribers (e.g., 90-day engaged) and exclude recent buyers or other inappropriate groups, not the full list.
cards.use_when: Setting up the audience for any campaign in Klaviyo, especially new product launches or promos where some subscribers shouldn't receive it.
steps: Create engaged-time-window segments earlier (prospects engaged 90-day example) and select them in the 'send to' field of the campaign — do not send to raw lists.

Use the 'don't send to' option to exclude subscribers for whom the message is inappropriate; for a new product launch, exclude anyone who purchased in the same category in the last 3 days by building that segment and adding it to the exclusion.
Where a campaign resends to a narrower segment, choose that narrower segment separately (e.g., only those engaged in the last 30 days) to avoid over-mailing lower-engagement people.
Check estimated recipients in the final review — Klaviyo shows it as the sum of included segments minus excluded segments.
Verify your segments are updating as expected: if you want exclusions to reflect purchases at send time, use the 'determine recipients at send time' toggle when scheduling.
caveats: If 'determine recipients at send time' is not ticked, dynamic segments are evaluated at scheduling rather than at the send moment — this is the wrong choice when excluding recent buyers.
The specific engagement windows (90-day, 30-day, 3-day) are examples from the walkthrough, not universal thresholds.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Decide smart sending per campaign, not just at account level
cards.summary: Override account-level smart-sending per campaign to control whether a subscriber who just received another email gets this one.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a high-priority campaign such as a big product launch or flagship promo, and deciding whether to let smart sending hold it back.
steps: Understand what smart sending does: it suppresses subscribers who recently received other emails so you don't over-send in a short window.
Set the baseline smart-sending limitations at the account level in settings, then override per campaign when the content justifies it.
Ask the specific question the presenter suggests: if someone received an abandoned cart email or a welcome series email within the last 16 hours, do we still want them to see this campaign?
For a big new product launch, the presenter's guidance is to turn smart sending off for that campaign because the subscriber is likely to want to hear about it; for routine content, leave it on.
After scheduling, confirm the smart-sending state in the final review screen — Klaviyo flags if it was disabled so you can verify it was intentional.
caveats: Turning smart sending off for every campaign risks over-mailing and unsubscribes; this override is reserved for genuinely high-relevance sends in the presenter's view.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Set up a new-product-launch campaign in Klaviyo end to end
cards.summary: Walk-through for building, templating and scheduling a new-product-launch campaign in Klaviyo with the correct audience, template source, tracking and timing.
cards.use_when: Building and scheduling a new product launch (or similar announcement) campaign for a Shopify store.
steps: Go to the Campaigns tab, create a campaign, name it (e.g., 'new product launch'), set the send date, set type to email, and add campaign tags — tags help with later data analysis.
Choose the audience segment (engaged segment) and apply any exclusions in 'don't send to'.
Turn smart sending on or off for this campaign depending on launch priority.
Include UTM parameters in tracking before moving on.
Choose the creative path: reuse saved templates, use the Klaviyo email library and edit, or start new — if you built the email in Figma, use 'create new' and drag in each image slice to rebuild it.
Write the subject line (intriguing, e.g., 'It's finally here...') and preview text (adds a second reason to open, e.g., 'the product that everyone's been asking for').

Use the campaign sequence builder to optionally add a follow-up resend, then review settings — estimated recipients, subject, preview, content, from/reply addresses, unsubscribe link (required for compliance), and tracking.

Schedule or send, choosing an exact send time (e.g., 9:00 a.m. Eastern when the product goes live on Shopify) or recipient local time zone, and toggle 'determine recipients at send time' if segments need to update at send.
caveats: Klaviyo's interface changes over time; verify current menu labels and toggle locations before relying on these steps.
The 9:00 a.m. launch-alignment timing is an example, not a rule — align send time with when the product actually goes live on your store.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Add a follow-up resend to catch non-openers
cards.summary: Resend a campaign to people who didn't open the first send, with a different subject line and a narrower audience, using Klaviyo's one-click toggle or manual cloning.
cards.use_when: Maximizing reach of a high-priority campaign such as a new product launch or a time-sensitive promotion.
steps: In the campaign sequence builder, toggle the resend to anyone who didn't open the first email.
Write a different subject line for the resend — if the first subject line didn't engage them, try another angle (e.g., 'Brand T-shirts just in time for summer').
Narrow the resend audience — for example if the first send went to a 90-day engaged segment, resend only to those engaged in the last 30 days to avoid over-mailing less engaged subscribers.
Set the time delay: Klaviyo will not allow a delay under 48 hours on the built-in resend.
For situations where you need faster or multiple resends, clone the campaign and send it manually instead of using the resend toggle.
caveats: The 48-hour minimum limit applies to the built-in resend feature — the presenter notes this is fine for non-time-sensitive sends but inadequate for fast events like Black Friday, where you clone and resend manually.
For Black Friday-type events the presenter suggests two or three resends of the same campaign to cut through inbox flooding — this is aggressive and should be weighed against unsubscribe risk.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Write copy that sells the click, not the product
cards.summary: For promos and launches, write email copy whose job is to get the subscriber to the website; education happens elsewhere.
cards.use_when: Writing a promo launch or new product launch email where the goal is to get subscribers clicking through to a product page.
steps: Recognize that the email's job is often to get the subscriber to the site — if they don't get there, they can't shop or buy.
Write copy that earns the click rather than fully selling the product in the email.

Use this especially when other campaigns or content have already done the educating — for example, a Black Friday promo email should just communicate the offer and get them out (Moment: 'up to 60% off sitewide, shop Black Friday deals').
Keep promo launch copy short and to the point — the presenter says the best promo launch campaigns are concise.
Ensure the destination (product page, collection page, landing page) carries the selling work, since the email is the doorway.
caveats: This is the presenter's recommended approach for promos and launches specifically, where awareness and interest already exist; for a cold or educational campaign, more explanation in the email may be needed.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Write to one core message per email and cut fluff
cards.summary: Confine each email to one (at most two) overarching themes and replace paragraphs with concise, scannable copy or icons.
cards.use_when: Drafting a welcome email, campaign or any email that is drifting toward a kitchen-sink of messages.
steps: Choose the single core message for the email — avoid the common mistake of packing a welcome email with bestsellers, FAQs, a founder note and reasons to love the products all at once.
Limit yourself to a maximum of one to two overarching themes across subject line, preview text and body.
Cut unnecessary words and avoid paragraphs — where an icon or visual element can carry the message, use it instead of a paragraph.
Remember that many subscribers won't read a paragraph — they'll see it, decide they don't have time, and move on.
Write consistently in your recognized brand voice once you've defined it — if you haven't defined it, get clear on who you are as a brand and who your customer is first.
Speak to your specific demographic rather than trying to be everything to everyone — messaging aimed at millennial women, for example, should use their language and their concerns.
caveats: The 'shorter attention spans' rationale is the presenter's assertion, not a cited study.
The one-to-two theme limit is a heuristic to improve clarity, not a hard technical rule.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Lead with benefits framed for your specific customer
cards.summary: Translate product features into the benefits that matter to your named audience segment, rather than repeating product details.
cards.use_when: Writing product copy for campaigns, subscription reminders or a new product launch where the subscriber needs a reason to care.
steps: Define the audience first (e.g., millennial women with kids vs Gen Z men) because the same product needs different benefit framing.
Convert product details into 'what's in it for them': instead of 'best beans grown in Ethiopia', say what the coffee does for the drinker.
Adapt the benefit to the audience: for a busy parent millennial woman, promote energy to get through the day; for a Gen Z male audience, promote productivity for late nights or energy for sports.
For a new product launch, ask 'why should they care?' and answer it explicitly in the email — do not leave the benefit only on the product page or packaging.
Example from the walkthrough (Moment, still orange drink): state the benefit plainly — fights stress, boosts mood, enhances focus — plus limited stock and a try-now CTA.
caveats: The examples are agency work shown in the course, not measured conversion results; the pattern is the transferable takeaway.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Subject lines and preview text: under 50 characters, frontload the value
cards.summary: Put the value in the first few words of the subject line, keep both under 50 characters, and use preview text to add detail or curiosity.
cards.use_when: Writing subject lines and preview text for any campaign where the subscriber sees only a truncated line in the inbox.
steps: Frontload the value: for a sitewide summer sale, do not write 'Summer's finally here, shop 50% off sitewide' — write '50% off sitewide' first, then use the preview text for the seasonal framing ('Summer's finally here, shop now').
Test that if someone only reads the first three words, they still understand the value.
Keep both subject line and preview text under 50 characters so truncation doesn't hide the offer.
Use preview text to complement the subject line with extra detail or a curiosity hook that gives another reason to open.
Don't over-invest in subject line perfection — the presenter says it is not the most important part of email marketing.
caveats: The 50-character guideline and the claim that subject lines aren't the most important part are the presenter's guidance, not measured benchmarks.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use persuasion levers: urgency, scarcity, social proof, curiosity gaps
cards.summary: Layer proven persuasion devices into email copy to increase the drive to act.
cards.use_when: Writing a promo, launch or content email and looking for a reliable way to increase clicks and purchases.
steps: Urgency and scarcity: state when a deal ends ('ends tonight') or that quantity is limited — the presenter says these reliably increase interest and action; use them only when true.
Social proof: feature customer reviews, user-generated content, influencer testimonials or press mentions — anything from a voice other than the brand increases subscriber trust.
Curiosity gap: tease content instead of revealing all of it; for a blog post, show a snippet and invite the click to read more rather than pasting the full post.
Place the persuader where it supports the CTA (e.g., urgency near the redeem-by line, social proof near the product or checkout module).
Do not fabricate what these devices assert — the persuasive effect collapses if the deadline or scarcity isn't real.
caveats: The presenter frames these as effective/common but does not cite measured lift numbers; treat them as well-worn tactics, not guaranteed uplift.
Fake urgency or invented social proof risks trust and compliance problems.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Design in Figma, not in Klaviyo's drag-and-drop
cards.summary: Build emails in Figma and slice them into Klaviyo rather than designing in Klaviyo's template builder, to get clearer offer communication, stronger structure and better visuals.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to design email creative before uploading into Klaviyo for a campaign or flow.
steps: Plan creative in Figma first; the presenter says strong layout and visual results shown in real examples are simply not achievable in Klaviyo's builder.
When uploading, in the campaign template step choose 'create new' and drag in your image slices one by one until the email is built.
The presenter's two structural reasons a Figma email outperforms: (1) structure and layout clarity, (2) the visual elements inside.
Don't conclude your brand can't support beautiful email design — the presenter's agency file shows strong designs for bold, natural, luxe, playful and educational brands.
After upload, verify the email renders with your brand fonts and that the layout is scannable on mobile, since sliced-image builds can be inflexible.
caveats: The presenter's comparative walkthrough (three Klaviyo-designed emails vs client Figma emails) is illustrative, not a controlled test with click or revenue data.
Sliced-image emails can hurt accessibility, text rendering, and load speed; this tradeoff is not addressed in the source.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Structure each email section as header, subheader, body, image, CTA
cards.summary: Use a scannable section hierarchy — header, subheader, optional body copy, image and CTA — repeated per section to funnel the reader to a click.
cards.use_when: Designing a campaign or flow email layout, especially one with multiple product or content sections.
steps: Give each section clear headers and subheaders so the subscriber can scan without reading every word.
Use enough white space so distinct messages read as their own sections rather than merging into a clutter.
Follow the order the presenter calls a top performer: header, subheader, body copy if necessary, image, and CTA.
If the section has multiple sub-sections, repeat that order within each one (as in multi-section client examples).
Think of the layout as a visual funnel: the header creates awareness (top), body copy educates and builds interest (middle), the CTA is the ask (bottom).
Test for scannability by asking whether a subscriber can see the offer (e.g., 15% off sitewide), the CTA, the merchandised favorites and the shipping USP without reading paragraphs.
caveats: The specific order is the presenter's recommended hierarchy, not a proved universal rule; variations work when all elements are still clear.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Three visual must-do's: CTA near products, icons not bullets, clear promo code
cards.summary: Place CTAs directly under each promoted product, replace bullet points with icons, and make the promo code unmissable near the CTA.
cards.use_when: Finishing email visuals before sending a promo, collection or product-focused campaign.
steps: Put a CTA near each merchandised product so a subscriber whose eye is caught can go shop immediately — don't rely on the product image being clickable, as many brands don't even link it.
Replace bullet points with icons (e.g., check marks) wherever the message allows — icons reinforce the point visually and are more engaging than a text list.
For promotion emails, make the redemption code unmistakable: put it in bold immediately before the CTA (e.g., 'use code SUMMER15 at checkout').

Watch for code placement that subscribers can miss — if the subject line says 25% off but the code is buried and 'Shop now' is the dominant element, subscribers will click without knowing they need a code and will be surprised at checkout.
Use only high-resolution imagery, and only relevant imagery: don't place an unrelated product image next to a product, and don't use a woman in the hero of a men's clothing email.
caveats: The warnings (missed code, blurred imagery) come from the presenter's inbox audit experience, not a measured test.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Monthly Klaviyo analytics audit: list growth, campaigns, flows
cards.summary: Run a monthly review of subscriber growth, opt-in sources and campaign performance to catch breakage and double down on what converts.
cards.use_when: The recurring monthly review of email channel performance and technical health.
steps: Check list growth: in Profiles, view subscriber growth over 30 days; note total subscribers, net change, new vs lost subscribers and month-over-month trend.
Drill into opt-in sources to see where subscribers came from (Shopify checkout and pop-up forms typically dominate) and their trends.
Diagnose a drop: a checkout-subscriber drop that matches a proportional drop in purchases/checkouts on Shopify is not a concern; a big gap between the two suggests the integration may be broken.
For a pop-up drop, open the form and compare views and submit rate across periods — if views fell but submit rate held or rose, the drop is traffic-driven, not form-driven.
Review campaign performance sorted by revenue for the last 30 days; then look at click rate (interest in content/offer) and placed order rate (what drove purchases).
Find the lowest performers and decide whether to cut, or — as with high-engagement newsletters — change the format to convert the engagement that already exists.
Review AB tests in the experiments section, and if needed end tests manually, keeping the highest converter.
caveats: The 27% month-over-month figure and other numbers are walkthrough examples, not benchmarks.
Sorting by revenue is the presenter's top-KPI recommendation, not the only valid view — open rate and click rate explain why revenue changed.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Read open rate, click rate and placed orders as a diagnostic layer stack
cards.summary: Interpret the three campaign metrics separately: open rate reflects subject line/targeting/timing, click rate reflects content and offer interest, placed orders reflect what drove purchase.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a specific campaign over- or under-performed and deciding what to change next time.
steps: Read open rate as a signal of subject line strength, targeting quality and send timing.
Read click rate as the metric for whether subscribers cared about the content and the offer — this is the metric to judge content/offer fit.
Read placed order rate (and revenue) as the indicator of what actually drove the purchase decision.

Expect divergence: a campaign can drive more clicks but fewer purchases (content is engaging but the reason to buy is weaker), and less-clicked campaigns can drive more revenue when the offer is a strong purchase moment (e.g., Father's Day gifting).

Use this reading to decide whether to fix subject line/targeting (low open), content/offer interest (low click), or offer strength (low orders), and check whether you're treating a high-engagement, low-revenue send (like a newsletter) as a failure when it's actually an audience-interest signal.
caveats: The presenter asserts benchmarks that you should at minimum see open rates above 30% and click rates above 0.5%, calling anything lower a likely deliverability problem; they also warn that universal benchmark numbers are not reliable without a deep account audit.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Use revenue and order count together to catch high-AOV distortion
cards.summary: Sorting campaigns by revenue can hide that a lower-revenue campaign drove more purchases; check placed orders and AOV before drawing conclusions.
cards.use_when: Analyzing top and bottom campaigns to decide which products, collections or campaign types to repeat.
steps: Sort campaigns by revenue first, since revenue is the primary KPI when the goal is revenue growth.
Then check placed order counts alongside revenue, especially for brands with high-priced, high-value products.

Note that a higher-revenue campaign can drive fewer purchases (e.g., $300 more revenue but 15 purchases vs 22 on a lower-revenue campaign), and the fourth-best revenue campaign can have the most unique purchases of the month.
If you're promoting products or collections that pull average order value down, the presenter suggests that may be a reason not to focus on them as much.
Combine this with click rate to understand whether the issue is interest or unit economics.
caveats: The specific numbers cited are from one walkthrough example, not general benchmarks; AOV distortion patterns vary by store.
Revenue remains the presenter's recommended first KPI — this card is an adjustment to, not a replacement for, that.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Diagnose a subscriber drop by separating traffic from form performance
cards.summary: When list growth falls, check whether the drop traces to site traffic decline (not controllable in Klaviyo) or form conversion decline (controllable).
cards.use_when: Monthly growth review shows a drop in new email subscribers and you need to decide whether to act on the form.
steps: Open opt-in sources and compare Shopify checkout subscribers and pop-up subscribers against Shopify purchase and checkout-started trends — a proportional drop suggests the integration and channel are fine.
For pop-up forms, open the form's reporting and compare form views and submit rate across the last 30 days and the prior 30 days.
If views dropped roughly 20% but submit rate rose from 2.19% to 2.28%, the subscriber decline was traffic-driven, not a broken form; the presenter treats this as no cause for concern.
Check whether the submit rate dropped dramatically, since form conversion is what you can control in Klaviyo — optimize here if it did.
Where form conversion is the issue, run or review an AB test on the form (the walkthrough shows an example test improving submit rate from 3.11% to 4.29%).
caveats: Submit-rate figures and the 20% view drop come from the walkthrough example, not a general benchmark; traffic attribution to paid/organic varies by brand.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Interpret Klaviyo's AB test statistics before trusting a result
cards.summary: Klaviyo surfaces a win probability and statistical significance but flags that test-period winners can differ from overall-send winners due to random chance, so extend or enlarge tests.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to call an A/B test campaign, subject line or flow variation a winner and roll it out.
steps: Open each AB test in Klaviyo's experiments section and read the lift in click rate, open rate or placed order rate and the win probability.

Watch for the case where one variation had the highest result during the test window but a different variation had the highest result overall on the full send — Klaviyo notes this can occur due to random chance.
When that happens, follow the guidance the platform gives: increase the length of the AB test period and/or increase the test size and rerun, taking the result with a grain of salt.
Manually end tests once a month when needed and keep the highest-converting variation.
Set up the next test each month regardless of outcome — the presenter argues that not testing means guessing about what your subscribers care about.
caveats: Klaviyo's statistics UI and recommendations may change over time; verify the current interface.
The presenter frames A/B testing as essential but doesn't establish a specific minimum sample size or duration.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Read top-level business review to attribute email revenue and understand month-over-month shifts
cards.summary: Use Klaviyo's business review dashboard to see total Shopify revenue, attributed email revenue, email as a share of revenue, and the campaign vs flow split.
cards.use_when: Reporting monthly email performance to the store owner and deciding whether growth came from campaigns or flows.
steps: Open dashboards > business review, set your time period and choose the comparison: previous period, or previous year if the brand is very seasonal.
Note total store Shopify revenue and its month-over-month movement.
Note attributed revenue and the percentage of total revenue coming from email — in the walkthrough example, just under 40% and up 9% month over month.
Open the message type breakdown to separate campaign revenue from flow revenue and their respective trends (example: campaign revenue $43K, up 54% month over month; flow revenue down 16%).

When a number moves sharply, dig underneath it — see the campaign revenue overview with conversion value, revenue and total recipients to understand what drove the shift, rather than reporting the headline alone.
caveats: The revenue figures and percentages are from one client walkthrough and are not universal benchmarks.
Attributed revenue depends on the attribution model in use; verify the model before presenting numbers as email's true contribution.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx

cards.title: Ensure every email adds value before it ships
cards.summary: Before scheduling any campaign or turning on a flow email, confirm it educates, entertains or solves a problem for the subscriber.
cards.use_when: Final pre-send check on any campaign or flow email to catch content that has no clear subscriber benefit.
steps: Ask the presenter's test question: why is my subscriber going to care about this, and will they be glad they opened it?
Answer against the three value types — does this email educate, entertain, or solve a problem?
If the answer is 'no' or 'I'm not sure', go back to the drawing board and rewrite rather than scheduling it.
Apply this equally to automated flow emails, not just campaigns.
Use the same question when assessing why a low-revenue but high-engagement newsletter performed the way it did — if subscribers enjoy it, change the format to drive revenue rather than cutting it.
caveats: The presenter's standard is subjective and their claim that new product launches are among the highest revenue campaigns is expressed as a personal guarantee, not a measured result.
cards.source_name: 2026 Klaviyo Email Marketing Full Course (3+ Hours).docx
